subtopic: BREAD FLOUR
BREAD FLOUR
speechtext:
1.	What substances are added to bread flour as improvers by milling companies?
2.	What quantity of these improvers was used for domestic consumption, during each of the past three years in Canada?
3.	Is bone meal added to bread flour? If so, in what quantities and for what purpose?
4.	What protein content is required for different grades of bread flour under the Food and Drugs Act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: BREAD FLOUR
speechtext:
1. The term "improvers" as used in the milling industry has meant bleaching agents and maturing agents. The term is no longer accepted by the department because its use is deemed to be misleading. Instead, millers are required to label flour in which bleaching agents have been employed, as "bleached". If maturing agents have been used, the statement "maturing agents added" must appear on the labels. These bleaching and maturing agents are permitted in all wheat flours. Some chemicals such as chlorine, chlorine dioxide and nitrosyl chloride are both a bleaching agent and a maturing agent at the same time, while potassium bromate, for example, is a bleaching agent only and ammonium persulphate is a maturing agent only. Section B.13.003 of the regulations under the Food and Drugs Act lists those substances which are considered to be bleaching and/or maturing agents, as follows:
(g)	oxides of nitrogen,
(h)	chlorine,
(i)	chlorine dioxide,
(j)	nitrosyl chloride,
(k)	benzoyl peroxide mixed with not more than six parts by weight of one or a mixture of two or more of
(i)	calcium carbonate,
(ii)	calcium sulphate,
(iii)	dicalcium phosphate,
(iv)	magnesium carbonate,
(v)	potassium aluminium sulphate,
(vi)	sodium aluminium sulphate,
(vii)	starch, and
(viii)	tricalcium phosphate,

Questions
in an amount not exceeding 100 parts of benzoyl peroxide for each 1 million parts of flour,
(l)	potassium bromate in an amount not exceeding 50 parts for each 1 million parts of flour, and
(m)	ammonium persulphate in an amount not exceeding 250 parts for each 1 million parts of flour.
It will be noted that limits are stated only for (k), (1) and (m) above; no limits are stated for the other substances since the amount of these latter chemicals that can be used is self-limiting at a very low level.
2.	There is no way of estimating the quantity of the ingredients which have been used for domestic consumption in Canada. Since the amounts of some are self-limiting and of others are limited by regulations, it is reasonable to assume that the total amount of these ingredients is very small in relation to the amount of flour produced. Generally, millers do not use more than one bleaching agent and one maturing agent in any flour and frequently one compound performs both functions.
3.	Under section B.13.004 of the regulations under the Food and Drugs Act calcium carbonate or edible bone meal in an amount that will provide in one pound of enriched flour not less than 500 milligrams and not more than 650 milligrams of calcium is a permitted addition. This addition is not compulsory. The addition of edible bone meal is required in Newfoundland. This is the only province in which such a law exists and it is designed to correct a local dietary condition. Enriched flour, supplied in the rest of Canada, does not contain edible bone meal or calcium carbonate, to the best of our knowledge.
4.	The regulations under the Food and Drugs Act do not specify the protein content for flour. This is considered to be regulated by the fact that "cleaned milling grades of wheat" are stipulated as the starting point for the manufacture of all types of wheat flour.

speechtext: May I ask the Associate Minister of National Defence the question which inadvertently I asked on motions yesterday, when you pointed out very kindly, Mr. Speaker, that that was not the right place to ask it? Has the minister any statement to make regarding the causes of and the losses resulting from the collapse of the new naval building at Halifax?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: COLLAPSE OF NAVAL BUILDING AT HALIFAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter relating to Defence Construction Limited. Early reports indicate that part of the roof structure and three walls of the storage and maintenance garage at H.M.C.S. Shearwater, Dartmouth, collapsed on Tuesday morning, February 2. A bus and several other vehicles were damaged. No personnel were seriously injured.
The cause of the collapse is not known. An investigation is being carried out by Mr. K. E. Whitman, consulting engineer of Halifax, who is a specialist in structural design of many years' standing. Officers of Defence Construction Limited and of the navy engineering division are collaborating with him in the investigation. The contract originally was for $279,000, I believe. The building is in two sections. One section is quite intact, that is, the section containing the machine shop. The storage section has collapsed apparently through the falling of one of the trusses. No one knows why it fell or what happened, but that is being ascertained by engineers.
The fact that the building was taken over by the navy almost on the day the truss collapsed is not material, because the contractor has guaranteed the structure for one year. It was a structure designed by the contractor who was both the engineer and the contractor on the job. I am stressing that the damage can be made good without loss to the crown. I may say that Defence Construction Limited, the organization that handled this contract for the government, has handled $512 million

worth of construction which already has been completed, and this is the first accident of the kind that I know of in the course of that program.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: COLLAPSE OF NAVAL BUILDING AT HALIFAX
speechtext: What was the type of construction; wood, brick or stone?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: COLLAPSE OF NAVAL BUILDING AT HALIFAX
speechtext: Reinforced concrete walls and laminated wooden trusses. The design of the trusses was approved here in Ottawa. I am quite certain that the truss itself was not defective. My own theory, which is only a theory without having any data as to the collapse, is that there must have been a defect in the fastening between the truss itself and the walls. However, that will be determined and the damage made good.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: COLLAPSE OF NAVAL BUILDING AT HALIFAX
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question? Has the contractor who was responsible for the construction of this building since been awarded a contract for another building for the navy and, if so, has that contract been held up pending investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: COLLAPSE OF NAVAL BUILDING AT HALIFAX
speechtext: No, sir, it has not. This contractor is well-known and, as I say, has carried out five or six million dollars worth of work for Defence Construction Limited. The erection of the trusses was sublet to an Ontario firm, which is also a responsible organization. As far as the main contractor is concerned, the firm has always been good for its liabilities and I am sure it will be for this. There is no reason to question their integrity.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: COLLAPSE OF NAVAL BUILDING AT HALIFAX
speechtext:
May I ask a
supplementary question? Is it a fact that during the course of the construction of the building in question representations were received from an engineering organization or association calling into question the particular method being used in connection with this laminated wood process?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: COLLAPSE OF NAVAL BUILDING AT HALIFAX
speechtext:
Not to my knowledge. Laminated wood trusses are widely used throughout Canada. They were used with success during the last war, and they are used, not only in government construction but in private construction. As I say, the firm that designed and built the trusses and was responsible for their erection is well-known in Ontario. I know of no representations of that type having been made.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Would he tell the house something of the actions of his representatives in the meetings they have had with representatives of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in relation to the pollution of the North Saskatchewan and also whether or not, in view of the dispute as to the responsibility being federal or provincial, his government has . given consideration to amending the Criminal Code in order to cover a situation such as this, as a means of arriving at a permanent solution?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: NORTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR FURTHER INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. gentleman for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. As I told him and the house the other day, the chief of the public health engineering division of the Department of National Health and Welfare went to western Canada to confer with the appropriate authorities in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I may say also that he has conferred with health authorities regarding the same problem in the province of Manitoba.
He advises that due to the complexity of the wastes being discharged into the North Saskatchewan river near Edmonton and the very small amounts of the various pollutants it has not been possible to determine the particular material or materials which are causing taste and odour problems in downstream water supplies. The low flow in the river at this time and the fact that the river is covered with ice are factors which are probably contributing to present conditions. The ice cover prevents oxidation of the pollutants.
The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) had asked privately regarding the situation at The Pas in Manitoba. I can say that the use of activated carbon at The Pas appears to have corrected the taste and odour problem. Lack of equipment and treatment facilities have prevented a similar solution at water treatment plants between The Pas and Edmonton. The city of Prince Albert has made arrangements to treat its water with fluorine

chlorine dioxide. Laboratory experiments have indicated that this treatment is effective in removing the objectionable tastes and odours.
With regard to my hon. friend's use of the word "dispute" as to jurisdiction, I must say that what I said the other day with regard to the competence of the particular authority in question does not, in so far as our relations with the provinces are concerned, justify, to the best of my knowledge, the use of the word "dispute". There is no suggestion on the part of the provincial authorities that the matter is not one within their jurisdiction. However, the matter is receiving continuous study on the part of the industries, the provinces and other interested parties and we have assured the provinces that we will be glad, within our constitutional authority, to continue to collaborate in the matter of providing whatever technical skill we have at our command.

speechtext:

department that my predecessor obtained the services of a firm of outside consultants. The postal officials recognized that with the growth of the service a greater measure of decentralization was desirable and that they had not sufficient time to devote to the task of making a survey of the organization and procedure without leaving undone some of the many daily tasks which require their personal attention.
I wish to make it crystal clear, beyond any possible misinterpretation, that there never was any question of maladministration or even of complacency on the part of the administrative officials. It was not any investigation of any wrongdoing or any lack of interest, but simply a request for a managerial report, a desire on the part of these administrative officials to ascertain if their ideas of development and decentralization were along sound business lines and in conformity with up to date practices. They wished to take advantage of the knowledge and experience and progressive methods possessed by outstanding business consultants as a consequence of their constant study and experience.
The fact is, as the report repeatedly states, [DOT]that the department is well administered and departmental officers have vigorously pursued a program of efficient operation over the years. What better evidence of this is required than the fact that during the past 20 years the volume of mail has increased by 178 per cent whereas the increase in total staff approximated 100 per cent? It is simply by good, hard-fisted administration, by scrupulous attention to every detail, that this has been made possible.
What is the reaction of my friends in the opposition to this unquestionably efficient administration? The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) states he has nothing but praise and commendation for the way in which those who are carrying out their daily routine of mail service have been performing their functions. He pointedly remarks that his criticism is directed to the administration of the department. Other members of the opposition refer to the need for a housecleaning of these officials, and make other similar unjustifiable comments. Is it not strange, however, that during the same debate, in fact on the same day, still other members of the opposition were most complimentary in their references to the efficiency of the postal department?
The Woods and Gordon company do make a number of recommendations. I shall deal with them in detail later, but before doing so let me stress that the report states that

many of the suggestions originated with the administrative officers at headquarters. Let me give you just one simple illustration of what was done by the departmental officials in the past, years before the survey was made. In the financial branch, on their own initiative and without any outside help, the officials replaced the old system of handling money order accounts which had been in effect for many years-incidentally, under both Conservative and Liberal administrations-by the new type of money order which effected not savings of hundreds 'of dollars, not even the $30,000 stressed by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton), but over $350,000 annually. Many other such developments had taken place long before the Woods and Gordon company were called in.
The department has developed the mechanical handling of mail to a degree which is not even approached by many other first-rank postal administrations. We are now undertaking research to take care of the sortation and letter distribution problems of tomorrow by the utilization of electronics. It will be some little time before the complete machine is built, but it is another indication of the efficiency and progressiveness of the postal officials. It was by this kind of administration that we were able through all these years to more or less balance our books and not come to parliament asking for rate increases when practically every other business in Canada was imposing increased charges as a matter of course.
As I have already mentioned, payments to transportation companies have increased some 72 per cent. The salaries of employees have increased 100 per cent. During that time the increase in postal rates, applied to the whole range of charges to the public, had been approximately 22 per cent. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) gave a clear indication of what is being done when he referred to the fact that many years ago the revenue at Brandon was $110,600, with 44 employees. Now, with revenue of $217,120, there are only 41 employees. Like comparisons can be made in other offices. It was this close attention to routine administration and improvements in procedure that made the savings possible.
It was this same close attention to administrative details which occupied the time of departmental officials to such an extent that they could not look around to explore every field of potential future savings. Is this a crime? On the contrary, I think it is indeed a solid tribute to the zeal, energy and capacity of those men who have given devoted and efficient service over the years, and whose

ability and loyalty to their duties some members of the opposition attempt to depreciate. May I again read what the Woods and Gordon company state on this point:
We have been impressed by the over-all efficiency of the department and the basic soundness of its organization and administration. Many of the proposals incorporated in this report were brought forward by them. A number of important steps have been taken in recent years to improve both the organization and the administration. Further improvements are under active consideration by your senior officials and some are in course of implementation.
The summing up in the report is to the effect that departmental officials, if given more help, can free themselves from a lot of routine and they, and they alone, can make the savings which the report holds out, not as an immediate possible benefit but one to be derived in future years. May I again emphasize that they do not at any point in the report, or in any conversations I have had with them, indicate that these savings are to be realized immediately. What they say is that we must be prepared to spend more money at headquarters and in the field to achieve returns in the way of good service and possible economies in later years.
For my convenience Woods and Gordon Limited prepared a brief summary of the organizational and administrative items in their report, with some related observations. With the same reservation I made concerning the tabling of the main report, I am tabling the summary now, as it is much easier to follow than the lengthy main report.

speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, referring to the report, it is true that 73 major and minor recommendations have been made. But to say only this is unfair and incomplete, as I have already indicated, because the whole truth is that of these 73 major and minor recommendations 59 have already been implemented in whole or in part, nine are still under study, four have been rejected as offering no economy or improvement, and one is a matter of government policy.
In some instances it will take several months before the changes are finally completed. In addition, there are recommendations which require further study before they can be adopted as a matter of general practice because, while commendable in their conception, they are questionable from the standpoint of practical application. We do not, however, discard any of these recommendations until we have examined them thoroughly. Thus the sweeping statements to the effect that efficient administration will permit us to make enough savings to meet the added cost are swept away by the facts.
The fourth main proposal of the opposition is that if we cancel subsidies such as franking, etc., we will not require added revenue. Before dealing with the abolition of franking may I briefly refer to subsidies, which I dealt with rather fully earlier. The opposition suggest doing away with the franking subsidies and, in the same breath, suggest that we should have kept the excise tax which was in itself a subsidy to the Post Office Department. They cannot be serious in this suggestion, because they are so inconsistent. Surely this inconsistency shows that they are both for and against subsidies. They want to have their cake and eat it too.
Dealing now with the suggested abolition of franking, may I say that even if this were done the revenues obtained in that way would cover only a small fraction of the total additional expenditures of $13,500,000. Hence this is another futile suggestion, which brings no remedy to the situation. Moreover, the opposition is only presenting one side of the picture. The principle of franking is to give free mail communication to those seeking, as well as to those supplying, administrative information. The franking privilege

Post Office Act
is given so that free mail communication may be established between the Canadian public, the ministers and members of parliament.
If we abolish franking in one direction, it is only logical to expect it to be abolished in the other direction. Otherwise one group could very easily place the other in an untenable position, and thus the flow of information could well become a trickle in one direction and a river in the other. In order to obtain free administrative information, franking must be maintained in both directions. If, on the other hand, the opposition want to abolish franking in one direction, they must expect it to be abolished in both directions. It is a two-way street.
Thus, while the opposition suggest that the franking privilege be abolished, they neglect to show that the Canadian public will then have to pay for all mail communications sent to their elected representatives. The members of the opposition, therefore, while appearing to oppose a necessary increase in postage rate, are themselves at the same time proposing a further increase in mailing cost to the public.
I shall now deal with some of the statements made by my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition. I am following this procedure because it will also answer many of the questions asked by other members of the opposition. The Leader of the Opposition makes comparisons with the rates paid in other countries. He points out that the rate in the United States is 3 cents, but he does not mention that the authorities in that country, as I have already indicated, are endeavouring to increase their letter postage rates and that there is under study a measure very similar to that which forms the basis for the present bill. This has already been covered by my reference to the message from the President quoted in Time. Neither does the hon. member draw to the attention of the house the fact that during the last fiscal year the United States post office department had a deficit of $770 million.
In making his reference to postage rates in the United Kingdom he compares the rates paid there on the basis of exchange rates, rather than in relation to the United Kingdom economy. A rate of 2\ pence in relation to the British economy is practically the same as 5 cents in relation to the Canadian economy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: For how many ounces?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
I am coming to that now. He mentions that this rate is for 2 ounces, but overlooks the fact that the maximum distance which a letter travels in the United

Kingdom is not more than 500 miles whereas in Canada it may travel three or four thousand miles, a large part of which is by air transport with no additional charge to the mailer. A fairer comparison would be the rate paid in Australia, where conditions in so far as distance is concerned more closely approximate those in Canada. In that country the rate is 3J pence, which in relation to the Canadian economy is 7 cents.
Moreover, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) said in the house that the rate paid on postcards in Poland is 6 cents and on postcards in Czechoslovakia, 5 cents. In addition, he said that the rates were much higher in Portugal, Egypt, and India. The figures I have for the United Kingdom and Australia, and the figures given by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, show very clearly the inaccuracy of the statement by the Leader of the Opposition "that we will have the highest postage rates in the world."
He also makes reference, as did previous speakers, to the penny postage introduced by Sir William Mulock. He fails, however, to make reference to the increase introduced by the Conservatives in 1915 or to the increase from 2 cents to 3 cents made by the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett in 1931, and this at a time when the country was suffering from a depression.
The Leader of the Opposition indicated that it would be quite reasonable for anyone close to the United States to carry their letters, which would normally be posted in Canada and deposit them in the United States post office, in order to take advantage of lower rates of postage. He even went so far as to say that there would be nothing illegal in this. I must issue a warning to those persons who might take seriously the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition. International postal regulations, to which every postal administration is signatory, expressly deprecate such a practice and specifically provide that the administration in which the letters are posted may either return the items in question to the country of origin or impose a surcharge equal to the amount of its internal rates.
The Leader of the Opposition made the statement that the government knew quite well when the excise tax on notes and cheques was removed that an increase in postage rates was to follow. I am rather surprised that my hon. friend would so disregard the facts. The first intimation of the discontinuance of the excise tax on notes and cheques was in February, 1953. The civil service commission did not commence the salary adjustment until sometime in the fall of 1953, and the first list of revised salary rates was

published on or about the 1st of December, 1953. Furthermore, no decision was given by the government in regard to the general adoption of the five-day 40-hour week in the operating service of the Post Office Department until sometime in September, 1953. The bill authorizing a readjustment of the rates for rural mail couriers did not become law until the 14th May, 1953.
I am, therefore, completely at a loss to know on what grounds the Leader of the Opposition could possibly justify the statement made by himself, and other members of the opposition, when items which occasion the additional expenditures were not even contemplated at the time the excise tax on notes and cheques was removed.
The hon. member states according to page 1152 of Hansard for January 15, 1954:
Surely we are not going to be told that there was no difference in the cost of the operation in the handling of the $7,500,000 worth of stamps.
Certainly there is a difference in the cost of operation, but not to the extent which the Leader of the Opposition endeavours to indicate. The actual cost of the stamps would be in the neighbourhood of $20,000, and the reduction in operating and distributing costs might be as high as $10,000, making a total of $30,000, which is somewhat far removed from the $7,500,000 which the post office has lost in the removal of this excise tax.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have again placed before the house most objectively the position of the government in regard to this bill. I have also answered all the major criticisms and many of the less pertinent comments of the opposition. I feel that this further constructive presentation shows without any doubt the soundness of the position of the government, and destroys alleged objections put forth by the opposition. I must say that the elementary principle that one thing cannot at the same time be white and black applies to everyone, and I am sorry to say that some members on the opposite side have sinned against this principle.

speechtext: Who is without sin?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
I shall not look at you.
May I give still another typical example of this contradictory attitude by referring to the speech made by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton) the other day, when, after having repeated for almost 40 minutes that the postal department should cut its expenditures, he concluded by asking that the same postal department spend $4 or $5 million more to give the service of a second delivery a day in residential areas. You cannot have it both ways. That is why
Post Office Act
I say that some of my friends on the opposite side have sinned against the principle that nothing can be white and black at the same time.
As I said a few minutes ago, we are all agreed that the additional expenditures of $13,500,000 are essential. There are two ways of obtaining the money to meet these additional and essential expenditures. One is by an increase in the postal rates; the other is by general taxation. So far I have not received from anyone in the house any other suggestion. We prefer the former. We feel that the cost of the service should be borne by the users and not by the taxpayers generally. We think this is an equitable arrangement. The opposition prefers the latter. They want to subsidize the service, with all the illogical and dangerous consequences to which I have already drawn attention.
The present issue is a clear-cut one. Foreseeable additional expenditures to carry out decisions already made total $13,500,000. The additional expense can be met either by taking it out of the general tax or by increasing postage rates. I recommend the straightforward approach so that the public will know exactly where they stand. I am of the opinion, as I have already indicated earlier, that the persons who use the service should pay for it, rather than that we should becloud the issue by subterfuge.
I know the measure is not a popular one in some quarters, but it is at least honest, and I am sure it will appeal to those members of the public who desire to pay their way rather than throw their burden on someone else.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with one statement and one statement alone of the Postmaster General I should think there would be agreement at this time, and that is that this problem should be discussed frankly. The speech we have just heard has followed the convenient practice-that is, convenient to some people-of attributing to members of the opposition statements they did not make, and then on that false foundation presenting an argument which had no relation to anything that had been said in this house in this discussion.
The minister has just read a tawdry political statement. It has been a review of political considerations which had no relationship to the immediate matter now before us. In fact, some of his statements reminded

Post Office Act
me very much of a quotation from "Alice in Wonderland" which I am sure he will recall:
When I use a word, it means just what I choose it to mean-neither more nor less.
The minister said that the opposition has suggested subsidies. Where has he found that? When the minister talks with horror of subsidies, will he explain to us how on the one hand he has such horror of something that was not suggested, while at the same time he conveniently overlooks the fact that the method he is proposing means a subsidy on a large scale to Trans-Canada Air Lines? The merits of that may be subject to debate on other occasions, but let the minister not suggest for one moment in this house that the proposal he is making is not a straight subsidy to T.C.A.
The minister has shed crocodile tears about the little man whom he is going to serve, as against the interests of the big man and the big business. He is doing the very opposite. What he is doing is charging the little man more than the big man who can use air mail, and get air mail service without paying for an air mail stamp. That is what he is doing. That really is exactly along the lines of the statement in "Alice in Wonderland" to which I have referred.
But, Mr. Speaker, there are other points that I should like to mention before I pass on to some of the subjects the minister discussed. He says that things cannot be black and white at the same time, and that it would be well if that elementary proposition were recognized. It would indeed. I want to speak about that. In tabling the memorandum prepared for him in December by J. D. Woods and Gordon the minister told us that he made it available to the house under the same terms as he made available the confidential report of J. D. Woods and Gordon.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have here the interesting question of when a report becomes confidential. I hold in my hand the report which has been under discussion, and I have not been able to find outside, back or front or inside, the words "personal, confidential" or anything that suggests that it is such. Again this bears repetition, because we see it in the words of the Postmaster General. What he tells us is that when he uses a word it means just what he chooses it to mean, neither more nor less. We do not need to attribute that to "Alice in Wonderland"; that is what the Postmaster General says. He says it is confidential; therefore it is. J. D. Woods and Gordon did not think of putting that covering restriction on it.

Again I express some surprise, Mr. Speaker, that what the minister regarded as a confidential report should have been so freely referred to in the statement made on behalf of the department, where it appeared it would be helpful to refer to it. Surely this is an elementary proposition, to use the term the minister used. If you use part of a document to support your argument, the whole document must become available. I know he will agree with me immediately in regard to that proposition. Therefore when the department sees fit to support its statement by partial reference to the document which was not marked "confidential", but which he says is, then we may ask ourselves, how are we to tell just which pages are confidential, which paragraphs, and so on?
The fact is that it is not confidential. It is part of the business of this house; it is part of the business which is to be attended to by the hon. members who are now able to devote more time to the business of the house or who will be able to as a result of the decision of a majority of the members within the past few days.
May I repeat that documents referring to administration which do not in some way affect security, or which do not in some way deal with matters that are subject to limitations of secrecy, are not in any way the private property of this government. One of the statements the minister made when he was setting up the false proposition was that we had criticized the appointment of this firm of specialists. I do not know where any such criticism was made. On the contrary, we have been urging that specialists in many lines be permitted to examine the organization of government and improve its efficiency, as we are confident could be done in many directions.
The minister made another statement that I should like to deal with before I pass on to something else. He referred to my remark about the invitation that this would offer in cities along the international boundary to firms and individuals to take their very large daily mailings across the boundary and buy stamps in the United States for 3 cents, which would perform the same service to any part of Canada as the 5-cent stamp would here after this bill passes. He said I had overlooked a provision in the departmental instructions where it is suggested that the department deprecates such a practice. Oh, we not only must abide by the law; we must abide even by the wish of this government. If the government deprecates, then nobody must do it. If the government deprecates, then that is enough to stop anybody doing it.

I just want to clarify that point.
I was talking about the universal postal union.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
I hope the people of this country will abide by the laws of Canada. The statement that somebody has deprecated a practice does not in any way affect the legality or propriety of anybody availing himself of such facilities as are presented in a perfectly legal manner. I would think most of us would regret if it became necessary or even desirable for anyone to go out of this country to get a service at 60 per cent of the cost he would pay for the same service here in Canada. This government are telling us about the need for continental integration, and surely they will recognize how readily it would fit into the picture of continental integration in business, in a very simple manner right across the border, if they invite this to be done.
I indicated quite clearly before that I did not think that would be a desirable situation. I repeat that there is no law against it. I also repeat, however, that if a service of that kind is available along the border it should be available everywhere else in Canada. It is not something that should be available to the few; and in this case it is not something that would be available to the little man about whom the minister professes to express such concern. It is something that would be available to the big organization which would find it useful and valuable where they were handling mail on a sufficiently large scale.
No, it is not big business or the person with lots of money who is affected adversely by this. It is the little man. Let me give an example, and I am ready to name the man who writes this letter, which is one of many that have come to me on this subject. It is written by a man named Harris.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext: Of Grey-Bruce?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
Not of Grey-Bruce; of Aylmer West. I shall simply read the first paragraph, which tells the story of the letter, and which is as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am a shut-in and very short of cash and I write a bit which is all I can do to put in time and a 5 cent postage means more cash and I have only $65 per month plus $2.50 interest to spend on household and the M.P.'s are increasing pay.
That is a comment by just one of the little men about whom the minister is expressing such concern. I submit that this expresses in simple terms the attitude of a great many little men in regard to the proposition now before us.
Post Office Act
This is not just something effecting an increase of 1 cent in the cost of postage; this is something that increases the cost of mailing generally, particularly to those people who find the mail a very useful means for the exchange of ideas. Again may I remind the minister that the little man cannot use the telephone and the telegraph as readily as big business or the person of substantial income, nor can he use it in the free and easy way in which the government does. The postal service is the means of communication of the little man, and the result of this change becomes a substantial total when every penny must be watched over the year in which letters are written.
The minister says that we have put forward four different propositions: One, that we take it out of general taxes; two, that we live off past surpluses; three, that there be an increase in administrative efficiency; four, that there be subsidies.
Only one of those is correct; only one of those even moderately resembles the arguments that have been made. We have urged that administrative efficiency be increased and that new methods be employed to seek a wider kind of service which would in itself increase revenue. The minister, in referring to Sir William Mulock, whose name has been mentioned on different occasions, pointed out that since that time increases have been made. That is true. However, he should recall that when Sir William Mulock decreased the cost of postage stamps it was not because of a decrease in the cost of living or in wages or salaries. He believed that there would be increased revenue which would make this possible, through the increased use of the mail as a result of the lower stamp charge. That in fact was the whole history of the use of postage stamps from the time they were inaugurated during the last century.
This is something that might well be considered now because of the fact that the department has cut out deliveries and has made the usefulness of the mail service much less apparent. There is a greater reliance on the telegraph and the telephone by those who can afford to pay for it, particularly by the government or contractors operating on a cost-plus basis.
We believe there can be an increased administrative efficiency. We believe that the J. D. Woods and Gordon report makes that perfectly clear. While pointing out quite frankly and most satisfactorily from the point of everyone that they found a commendable measure of efficiency in the general administration, at the same time they pointed out

Post Office Act
many things that could be done and many specific things that would effect very substantial savings in themselves.
Just to deal with the four points that have been made, I do not recall the suggestion that it would become necessary to take this out of general taxes, if proper methods were employed. Then so far as living off past surpluses is concerned, my impression was that when the surpluses were referred to it was to emphasize that there had been deficits before and that following those deficits there were again surpluses for varying reasons, we will hope either because of new methods, increased efficiency or the increased use of the mail service.
Certainly my contention in pointing out the very large surpluses which had been accumulated was to suggest that when those accumulated surpluses became a deficit in a single year on this occasion, it should not cause any more concern than the deficits which had occurred twice in the past 30 years and which were followed immediately by substantial surpluses. My own conviction is that if the department will put into effect the recommendations of the J. D. Woods and Gordon report and will seek to supply a wider and more frequent mail service by many devices not yet employed but which are available elsewhere, in the immediate future that deficit might well be followed by surpluses once again. We believe there is no necessity to suddenly jump at this large increase because of the immediate increase in expenditures, without first testing other methods of meeting that cost.
The minister has said everyone agrees that the additional $13,500,000 must be paid in this way. Everyone does not agree. I do not agree; I do not believe most hon. members on this side agree, and I am inclined to think many hon. members on the other side do not agree either that this is necessary. Of course that $13,500,000, if that is the correct figure, will have to be met, as other increases will have to be met from time to time. But what we suggest is that there are different ways in which this can be done.
Let us see what some of the points are that might well be given consideration. The J. D. Woods and Gordon report was, after all, simply dealing with administration, and suggests methods of improving that administration. It did not come within the terms of their reference to make suggestions regarding policy. That is something which seems to have been overlooked by the minister. When they did not suggest changes in policy, that does not mean they did not think there might not be changes in policy.

If they had been asked to recommend changes in policy doubtless they could have suggested certain changes.
They simply made passing reference to possible consideration of the fact that other departments are not paying for their services. When we begin to examine the subject we learn that the Post Office Department gives free service to other departments amounting to $4,700,000. But these other departments pay for their telegrams, and pay their telephone bills. They pay for other services they obtain. It would seem to me that good government accounting would suggest it would be advisable that these other departments pay for their postal service. After all, the public in the end is going to pay for this one way or another, and it would leave the actual departmental costs on a much more realistic basis. At any rate, there should be an examination of that fact before there is any suggestion that we simply go right ahead and meet that $13,500,000 by increased postage rates.
There is another figure that has been under consideration. The minister said we claimed that the stamp tax should not have been taken off. I do not recall when that was argued. What was suggested, and what I repeat, is that unless the government is even more inefficient in every department than we believe it is-and we certainly believe it is very inefficient in many-then it certainly knew when it took off the stamp tax what that would mean in loss of revenue to the postal department. That was what we said. What we pointed out was that at the time they took that tax off they claimed the credit for doing so, but offered no indication to the people that this would have to be paid for in the way it is now being paid for.
An election intervened. They told the public what they were doing, but they neglected to tell them they were going to claim later on that they would have to meet the cost in some other way. Do not let the minister suggest that the postal department was not aware of this. That would be an infinitely more serious indictment than anything yet put forward in this house. It would mean a complete lack of realism in their approach to the examination of their revenues. No, Mr. Speaker; the proper method would have been to indicate that this was going to have that effect and to have made the adjustment at that particular time within the Post Office Department to compensate for it.
I also pointed out that this $7,500,000 is not all lost revenue. Let us see just what that proposition means. That $7,500,000 represents the sale of stamps that would have

gone on cheques if the law had remained as it was. Does the minister suggest that his department is so organized that it can sell $7,500,000 more stamps without any extra cost? To put it the other way, does he believe that the selling of $7,500,000 less in stamps means no saving in the cost of operation? That surely would be an indictment of the organization within his department. I do not believe anything of the kind, and I do not think he does. We have had no figure yet of what the net result would be, but that is a balancing saving which could be put against that amount.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there are the specific recommendations in the J. D. Woods and Gordon report. With all the complimentary- and properly complimentary-things said, the report states this:
On the basis of extensive tests we believe that the addition of staffs trained in time and motion study and in the design of equipment should result in improved operating methods and substantial savings in costs.
The minister says it has not been possible to introduce some of the new machinery, but let us hope that this will become available during the current year. Certainly the present increase in postage rates, which would be inclined to become permanent now, should not pay for a temporary situation which can be changed by the acceptance of that recommendation and the savings that would result.
I am not going to deal with the recommendations into research and planning and various things of that kind, all of which have their impact upon operations, but another recommendation in the J. D. Woods and Gordon report is this:
The operations of the post office savings bank should be discontinued or restricted in the interests of economy. The bank was established originally to meet certain needs of the public which can now be taken care of by other institutions.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is an interesting and well-known history in regard to this. In the early days of this type of post office savings bank there was not the general service of banks that we have today. When this system was introduced in England with exactly the same name it was to meet the absence of local services. In a large measure the same arguments prevailed here. Today there is hardly a little community that has not satisfactory banking services; and certainly with the increase in the number of automobiles and buses and better transportation facilities of that kind, banking services are within the reach of everyone who wishes to use them. Here is a
Post Office Act
recommendation which would make a positive and definite saving if it were carried out. The report states:
If it is decided to wind up the post office savings bank there would be an estimated annual saving of $377,000 per annum and the field organization would be relieved of much detailed work.
That amount of $377,000, Mr. Speaker, is not very much to this government which has symbolized or epitomized its view on that subject by the classic expression, "what's a million, anyway?" Nevertheless $377,000 is just one item.
I come now to the specific references to the departments:
The department-
That is the Post Office Department.
-is required to bear the cost of mailing privileges granted to other government departments and of carrying out government policy in connection with the subsidization of transportation-
Oh, that horrible word; that word which so alarms the minister when he thinks somebody else used it, although he did not. To continue the quotation:
-the transportation of certain classes of mail at rates which are below cost and the operation of various services such as the post office savings bank.
Then another quotation; and may I say that these are only samples of some of the recommendations.
Primary sortation is the first division of unsorted mail into a number of different groups. While this plan will require further development there is an indicated annual saving in the forward letter section of the Toronto post office alone of approximately $200,000 per annum.
Then the next one I should like to read is this:
It is apparent that one of the major fields for economy and improvement in service open to the department lies in modification of the transportation facilities and methods used for distribution to the areas surrounding the larger cities.
What that merely means is this. Let the post office keep up with the times. Let the post office recognize that conditions are changing and that there are many means by which distribution and collection can be facilitated which they have not even tried or attempted to try, so far as anyone knows.
Then let me give one other quotation:
While these suggested revisions in the organization structure of the transportation branch do not materially change the administration functions, they strike at the primary weakness-the lack of future policy and program regarding the extent and nature of transportation services.
Then from appendix "A" may I read these words:
The saving of $850 a day or, say, $250,000 a year would appear to be a conservative estimate.

Post Office Act
May I say that is a small "c", Mr. Speaker; nevertheless it is obviously not the estimate put forward by this department. Going still further, and placing it on a still more conservative basis, the report says:
Although no detailed costs are available, it would not be unreasonable to expect that the initial capital outlay would be paid for within a year and thereafter there would be an annual saving of $200,000 a year.
Mr. Speaker, these are only some of the recommendations, and these figures I have been referring to have been directed to only one area and to one municipality with regard to increased efficiency. They could be extended right across the country. Mr. Speaker, now that it is convenient I am directing my remarks to the minister. I was pointing out that there are many ways in which mail delivery could be stepped up by the employment of modern devices which are becoming available in increasing numbers and variety, and which are employed with such satisfactory results in many large industrial units whose plants are spread over wide areas. Devices useful in one area might not be useful in another, but certainly consideration should be given to some of these things.
The minister has quite incorrectly attributed to the opposition suggestions they never made. I am not going to comment on that or even say what I think about it. I am simply pointing out that the minister has suggested a number of propositions which were not put forward. Let him deal specifically with the points that have been made. Let him indicate to us how far he is prepared to go in examining new methods for the speeding up of delivery by mechanical and other devices now available.
The history of postal service has been a history of improved service in most organized communities. In some of the larger cities of the world today there are several deliveries every day. Many people in these larger communities seldom think about using a telegram within their communities, because in some cases a reply may even be received by mail the same day. That has been the history of the development of efficiency and the encouragement of the use of postal service. It does not increase the desire to use the mail for business and other purposes, if other methods are open, when the service is cut to once a day. The fact that mail is only picked up once a day and only delivered once a day

Post Office Act
often has the effect of delaying for two days mail that otherwise would have been received within 24 hours.
No one is more anxious than I am to see that genial smile on the face of the minister who is presenting this bill, but may I suggest that if smiles are to be found on both sides of the house he should not in future attribute to members of the opposition motives or statements such as were contained in the presentation he read to us this afternoon, and which I believe on re-examination he will agree do not correctly interpret the statements made by myself or other members of the opposition.
We are dealing with something that is related to our whole society. We are dealing with the oldest form of communication. The life of people throughout the whole of recorded history is set out in letters that have been preserved. There you find frank and uncensored opinions. You find the attitude of the people of the time with respect to both sides of a question. We find not only inspiration but much of the history of Christianity itself in the letters of St. Paul. We find the other attitude, the other side of the story, in the letters of the emperors and officials of the time who were opposing the expansion of Christianity. Right throughout we find the way people thought and acted disclosed in their letters. We find many of those little things that indicate how life carries one along some path. In looking for a quotation that I might use to deal with the situation, I happened to find a quotation from Pliny the Younger. Obviously, he had not been getting as many letters as he thought he should, and Pliny the Younger said in a letter addressed to his son:
There is nothing to write about, you say. Well, then, write and let me know just this,-that there is nothing to write about;
From letters we can find how little life changes, and sometimes how little boys change, no matter how greatly the surrounding circumstances may change. That very wise, but not always acceptable writer, Voltaire, said that the post is the consolation of life. The old man who wrote the letter from which I quoted today was implying the same thing. Then, I recall the words of William James: "So long as there are postmen, life will have zest."
I do not suppose there is a single home where the arrival of the postman is not an exciting point in the day. I do not suppose there is a family where the arrival of the postman does not offer encouragement, and some news of their friends or relatives which is greatly enjoyed. An increase in that service

is not only to be desired from the point of view of encouraging the use of the mail, but it is part of our society. I believe, on the one hand, we would be serving our people well by trying that out and by returning to multiple services. We would also be following ordinary business methods by encouraging more business, and in that way getting more revenue.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this is a case that we should look at from the point of view of business, and the point of view of the relationship of the postal service to society itself. Before we are asked to impose this burden on the little man, for the benefit of those who will get free air mail service, I believe, on the one hand, we would be serving our people well by trying that out and by returning to multiple services. We would also be following ordinary business methods by encouraging more business, and in that way getting more revenue.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this is a case that we should look at from the point of view of business, and the point of view of the relationship of the postal service to society itself. Before we are asked to impose this burden on the little man, for the benefit of those who will get free air mail service, I suggest we should have much more information before us than we have. Without any more information than we have before us now, it is certainly my intention to oppose this bill.

speechtext:
Obviously, the minister is going to have a rather rough time with this bill. He is suffering, of course, for the sins of his colleagues, and he understands that. He grieved publicly in his first few words when he said that the arguments of the opposition had been repeated over and over again. He is quite right. We have repeated them over and over again, but how can we possibly get them to enter into the heads of hon. gentlemen opposite unless we do? We have been singularly unsuccessful. I have a feeling that the minister takes the position that since he has made up his own mind, he is now quite prepared to listen to reason. For the next few minutes I hope to speak in terms of reason as to why we are going to oppose this legislation.
We have already made it clear that we are going to do so. The minister has not advanced as yet an adequate case which would lead us to support it, nor has he given us reasons which we think are valid. The position that has been taken is that the principal cause of the deficit in the postal department this year is the advent of the five-day 40-hour week, the increase in salaries and the increases to contractors. I think it is specious reasoning.

Why is it that the employees of an organization must always be blamed for any increase in costs? Is there not another reason behind it? Is it not the fact that before the election this government removed a tax which resulted in a substantial loss of revenue to the post office? Is it not a fact that after the election the same government is imposing the tax, but in another area? Had that tax not been removed originally, there would have been no reason for the minister coming here today with this bill.
The minister maintains that a public service should pay its way. I do not think there is consistency in that position as between the minister and his colleagues. After all, why should the post office be the only department which is expected to pay its way? It is true it is providing a service, and that service must be paid for somehow or other. I think, for instance, of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), who has a department which provides a very important service to the people of this country. It is a service which is called upon frequently. It is used widely, and yet those who use it are not asked to pay the costs of the Department of Labour.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has a department whose services are used throughout the country, and rightly so. Those who use the services of that department are not expected to see that the departmental books are balanced at the end of each year. The minister states that the people who use the service should pay for it, and he regards it as a principle. Is he suggesting he is the only principled member of the cabinet? Is he suggesting the Minister of Labour is unprincipled because his department does not pay its way? Is the Minister of Trade and Commerce unprincipled because he does not make his department pay on the basis of public service?
What about the Minister of Public Works? He is in charge of a development which provides a service to the people of Canada, a means of communication, the trans-Canada highway. Are the users of it the only ones who shall be expected to pay for this service? Is there a principle there, or is the Minister of Public Works again one of my hon. friend's unprincipled colleagues? The minister stands above and far beyond any of them on the basis of his own arguments concerning principles.
Perhaps there is another reason for the deficit. Again, I am going to bring up this dreadful word "subsidies". The fact is that the imposition of this tax is going to penalize those who use the first-class mails of this country, and none other. There are deficits occurring in the post office because of hidden
Post Office Act
subsidies. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) pointed out when he spoke that there is a hidden subsidy to the newspapers in this country in the form of mailing privileges. As he argued, and as I argue, why should that subsidy be borne by the post office? Why should that subsidy not come out of the consolidated revenues of the country, instead of asking one group in Canada, the users of the first-class mails, to pay for it?
The minister used the word "equitable" in this respect, and he considers this legislation is equitable. He said the cost of the service should be borne by the users. The fact is, however, that the cost is not being borne by the users; the cost is being borne by only that particular group using the first-class mails. That is not equity, and that is not fair. Were the cost to be spread across the whole population, then perhaps there would be a different approach to this subject. One of the newspapers which, of course, benefits from this hidden subsidy is one which a person would expect would protest most loudly against it. In Winnipeg, we have the Winnipeg Free Press which, on past occasions, has opposed all manner of subsidy to anyone else, but of course not to itself. I see no reason why I, as an occasional user of first-class mail-I say "occasional" because most frequently I use the frank-should have to help subsidize the Winnipeg Free Press. I agree that it might be unfair to ask the small storekeeper to subsidize the large operator of the mail order system, but any subsidy in the Post Office Department should come out of the consolidated revenues and not be charged against one particular group.
In this particular respect I should like to know, and perhaps the minister can enlighten us later, what is the actual cost of delivering a letter which goes by first-class mail. I know that in the United States the cost is a little over 3 cents. It would be very interesting to know what the cost is in this country. We should then be in a position to find out how much the users of first-class mails are going to subsidize other users of the postal system in this country.
There is another matter which I should like to bring up. It concerns a type of inefficiency which we find in the post office organization. It is not an inefficiency amongst employees; it is not an inefficiency in the staff anywhere. I, in common with all others, receive my mail; be it rain or shine, be it 40 below or 100 above, I get my mail. I have no complaint in that regard; I have written to the postmaster in Winnipeg asking him to thank the staff for the help they have given. But there is still inefficiency in the post office, and there always will be inefficiency as long as the post

Post Office Act
office is used as the medium of political patronage. That is happening today. And when you get politics interfering with the administration of the post office, there, I fear, you are going to get unwarranted expenditures at the cost of course of the public.
There is a situation which exists just now in Winnipeg, and if the government would capitalize on it they could perhaps get some revenue, but I suggest it would be revenue taken in a most iniquitous way. This is actually what happens, and this is what leads to inefficiency in the post office. I have already taken the matter up with the department. This particular case will not be new. There is a drug store at Inkster and Main in north Winnipeg which has been a sub-post office for over 40 years. As an institution people know it is there. They are well looked after; the service is good.
One of the prominent members of the Liberal party in Winnipeg went to this drug store some months ago and said to the druggist: "You realize this drug store has been here for a long time and there is some rumour that there may be a change." I should say there had been a change in the ownership of the drug store. The new owner was an ex-serviceman who had fought for his country, and when he came back he bought the drug store and of course got the sub-post office, after the department had approved of the change. Since he was somewhat worried, the druggist, Mr. Chapman, went to see this prominent gentleman who had approached him and said: "What exactly do you mean, sir?" He was told that it was an expensive thing carrying on a political party. The Liberal said: "We need money; you have had the drug store for a long time. There might be a change, but I think the change could be averted if you could pay us the sum of $500." I am not saying that in north Winnipeg $500 is the usual price. There are some who pay only $200, but I imagine it ranges from $200 to $500 for the right to have a sub-post office. Is that the right way and the efficient way to go about creating a public service?
I have been approached, and I am sure other hon. members have as well, to assist somebody in getting a sub-post office. I do not know why they would possibly want it. I can conceive of it as being nothing but a headache, but they want it. I have said: "The department itself must decide, but I would suggest to you that you put in your store forms of petition asking people who come in to sign to the effect that they would like to have a sub-post office there. Then when you have enough names, send them in to the department and let it decide." Surely that

is the reasonable way of going about it, because the department must know better than anyone else whether or not there should be a sub-post office in that location. But it does not happen that way.
During the election a druggist quite near to my committee room came to me and said that the post office had taken away his subpost office. I found out the reasons why. They were perfectly proper. There was a change of ownership, and the post office naturally closed down the sub-office so that an audit could be made and an accounting could be taken. This man wanted a sub-post office and he approached me. I telephoned about his case to the head of the postal department in Winnipeg. A day or two later, knowing that it would not be an infraction of the law in any sense whatever, I took into this drug store a couple of C.C.F. window cards. The druggist put them in his window; that was all. The next day I went around and I found that the cards had disappeared and Liberal cards were in their place. Being somewhat intrigued I went to find out why and I was told that my Liberal opponent had gone into that drug store and had said: "Now, look here, do you want to get the sub-post office back? If you do, take the C.C.F. cards out and put Liberal cards in their place." I was not prepared to argue. The whole business was utterly absurd but it was the culminating act of many. That day, or the day after, I sat down and dictated a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), a letter which I never sent for the simple reason that on the day I dictated it the subpost office was granted. This is what I had to say. Since I was prepared to send it, I think I should be prepared to read it. It is dated July 22, 1953, and reads as follows:
The Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent. P.C.
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. St. Laurent:
I have already complained to the Postmaster General of cases of unmitigated blackmail on the part of some of your supporters in Winnipeg.
I consider it blackmail when a person has to pay to render a public service. I continue with the letter:
There has been no action yet that I know of.
A Winnipeg man has applied for a sub-post office in his drug store at Mountain and Main in this city. Money has already been demanded from him by members of the Liberal party for the favour. The public need apparently does not enter into the picture.
The druggist had one of my election cards in his window. My Liberal opponent went into the drug store this morning and insisted that my card be removed immediately and his substituted. The druggist was warned that if he did not do so, the recommendation for the sub-post office would be cancelled.

I call this blackmail. It is a form of venality which has no place in public life in Canada and I would like to know within the next few days what is going to happen to this man's application for a sub-post office if he keeps my card in his window.
I cannot see for the life of me how the post office can assert its efficiency when certain areas are so dependent upon political pressure. The sooner that type of pressure is taken off the department the sooner will it be the efficient vehicle which we hope it can become. We in the C.C.F. are dissatisfied. We are dissatisfied with the measure which is before us. We cannot agree with the suggestion which has been made that there should be an increase in rates, because we see no justification for the increase either in reason or in logic. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher):
That Bill No. 168 be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house a parliamentary committee should be established for the purpose of making an inquiry into the organization and operation of the Post Office Department and the postal services of this country.

In
the few brief months that I have been in this house it seems to me that one chief topic of debate has been increases. Here, there and everywhere, we are talking about increases for the unfortunate taxpayers.
Since this bill came forward I have had a good many letters from people in my constituency. They have not been letters from angry taxpayers, and they have not been anti-government letters, but I have found them pitiable and bewildering letters. Most of them are from old age pensioners. They tell me that when you have to live on $40 a month this extra penny becomes a real burden.
Post Office Act
The minister told us today that the government does not believe that the Post Office Department should live off general taxation because that would mean that those who do not use the mails would be paying for those who do. I agree with that viewpoint, but I go further. Surely there are other ways of increasing postal revenues. This general increase certainly hits what the minister calls the little man far more than it does those who can afford it. As my leader said earlier, the little man is subsidizing the carrying of air mail more cheaply for the big man.
I suggest that one way in which revenue could be raised is to put the stamps back on cheques. Those who can afford to write cheques can certainly afford to buy stamps, whereas those who have to live on $40 a month simply cannot stand this extra burden. I would suggest that the seven-cent air mail postage be maintained. Those who want speedy delivery of their mail can afford to pay for the privilege.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) has called this a back-handed subsidy to the T.C.A. Why should those who cannot afford the luxury of the T.C.A. be asked to pay this subsidy? Let those who want speed pay for it.
Truth to tell, I view with some skepticism the worthiness of the claim of speed and efficiency in our air mail service in Canada. In increasing the postal rates the minister offers us something of a sop when he says that he is decreasing air mail rates. I must say that he presented this sop in a most beguiling way. He told us that the air mail rate would go down to five cents and that, wherever it was expedient to do so, letters would be carried air mail whether they were so designated or not.
I do not feel too happy about this promise. The other day the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) said that we wanted to do everything too fast, that we want a letter to reach its destination just a few minutes after we have written it. That of course is unreasonable. I have here three envelopes which were mailed from Toronto addressed to Woodstock, New Brunswick. Ordinarily these letters would take two and a half or three days to go from Toronto to Woodstock, New Brunswick. There was no extra postage on them, just the four-cent stamps, but they went air mail with speed and dispatch. In fact they went at such speed and dispatch that it took them 11 days to go from Toronto to Woodstock, New Brunswick. An interesting thing about it is that they went around by Goose Bay, Labrador, in order to reach their destination.

Post Office Act
I wonder if the minister would consider a pithy little suggestion which a Toronto writer put forward the other day. Perhaps he would put out a six-cent stamp which would provide that the envelope would go by train only. This business of having our letters go air mail whether we want it or not is not always to our own advantage.

I am opposed to this increase in the postal rates. I am not even convinced that it is necessary. One hon. member called it a preventive measure. If the Post Office Department needs increased revenues they should put the stamps back on cheques. I know it is a nuisance tax but there will not be an election for at least four years and they can get away with it for that long.
The cheque stamps would be a nuisance but they would not be the hardship to anyone that this general increase will be. I suggest also that we keep the extra two cents for air mail postage and let the T.C.A. woo and win its own customers instead of having them handed to them on a silver platter. Let us not allow one of the most important facets of Canadian life, the means of communication, to become a luxury instead of the right of every citizen rich or poor. For that reason I am opposing this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I want to add a few words at this time in support of the amendment before the house. I believe this amendment, which calls upon a committee of this house to obtain the fullest possible information on the operations and administration of the Post Office Department and for the bringing in of recommendations that might be of assistance in providing more efficient postal services, is vitally necessary at this time. If I was not in favour of the amendment before then, the speech of the Postmaster General convinced me that it is necessary, because the more he spoke the more confused the entire situation became.
I believe his proposals are contradictory. This afternoon, for example, the minister time after time reiterated that those who use the mails must pay for them. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that until he has demonstrated that the principle which he enunciated is in effect, then he has no business whatsoever in asking this house to authorize an increase in postage rates. The minister is definitely putting forward a basic principle which he himself knows is not in effect, because those who use the mails in all categories are not paying for the services they receive.
I am not going to take up the time of the house in expounding at too great length what has already been mentioned by several

speakers this afternoon, namely, the matter of second-class mail. If the minister is correct in his assertion that those who use the mails should pay the costs, then he ought to carry through his own contention and make those who use the second-class mail carry the second-class costs. If this were done I am convinced, from what I have heard, that there could not possibly be any deficit in the coming fiscal year.
As regards the minister's contention that those who use the service should pay, I want to add my voice in support of those who have already said that the various departments of government should not have the right of using the frank, which admittedly is a charge of $4,000,000 on the Post Office Department. That $4,000,000 is for administrative costs of government itself and administrative costs of various departments and it should honestly be charged as such. If that were done, there would be an immediate saving of $4,000,000- I believe that is the correct figure-on the charge for postal services.
There is another angle of this phase of the department's operations and that is this question of franking privileges. I am convinced an examination of this question would not only place the postal service in its right perspective, but would also save the taxpayers of this country a great deal of money. I have been absolutely amazed in the time I have been here, since becoming a member of parliament, at the terrific amount of mail I receive from government departments. I would make a bet, if it were legal to do so, that if a check were made on the waste-paper baskets in members' offices this very evening there would be found such a stack of envelopes and discarded material from government departments as to astound everyone. I have spoken to member after member and they have told me they have reached the point now where they do not even bother to open much of that mail but simply tear it in half and throw it in the wastepaper basket.
