Mr. Speaker, the speech of the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote), supplementing the remarks made when a resolution calling for an increase in postage rates was presented to this house, has little to commend it because the minister failed to establish by facts and figures his contention that the increase is necessary.
According to the Postmaster General the estimated deficit for the department will amount to $7,500,000 through the loss of revenue due to the cancellation of the excise tax on stamps for use on cheques. He estimates that there will be a $5,000,000 deficit due to the adoption of the 40-hour week; $7,000,000 due to the increase in wages of general post office staff; $1,500,000 due to an increase to rural mail couriers; and approximately $1,000,000 covers increased awards to railway companies. All these estimates belong in the realm of conjecture.
The addition to post office revenue of moneys arising from excise stamps on cheques was unwarranted, for this tax had its proper place in the consolidated revenue fund. To suggest the inclusion of the receipts from this tax in a post office department surplus or deficit was entirely wrong in the first place, and the only conclusion that can be drawn is that it was an indirect way of supplying the funds that were necessary for subsidies and subventions within the department. It is now apparent that these concealed subsidies will have to be paid from the consolidated revenue fund and not from postal revenues.
As to the deficit attributed to salary increases, it is quite evident that the predicted deficit will disappear through the normal expansion of business which, according to the department's own figures, shows an average increase per annum of $4,100,000 and which in turn exceeds expenditures by $100,000 per annum.
Further support for the claim that the government has blundered in proposing increased postal rates at this time may be found in the J. D. Woods and Gordon, Limited, report, which was so abridged in the Postmaster General's report that one could only obtain the gist of its content. After reading a major portion of this report I came to the conclusion, as many hon. members have surmised, that the department has allowed the perfection of its service to deteriorate because of inadequate staff and equipment, and

Post Office Act
that an overburdened staff could not cope with the demands of an expanding economy and an increased population.
It is my contention that the department has only to put into effect the recommendations of the report in order to return to its previous halcyon days. Had the government made a sincere effort to study this report they would have found it a veritable gold mine of useful suggestions, observations and recommendations. It clearly points the way for the pay-your-way advocates. Here are a few comments from the preamble to the survey. I am quoting from page 11:
We have been Impressed by the over-all efficiency of the department and the basic soundness of its organization and administration.
The Leader of the Opposition drew attention to that quotation. But page 12 contains this, and I quote:
Prior to war, the services were steadily expanding. During the war the expansion accelerated and has continued at an ever-increasing pace. The established policy of successive governments was that expenses should be kept within the confines of postal revenues.
That expenditures on salaries and services have increased substantially since 1945.
There was also a substantial increase in the volume handled.
On page 13 the report continues:
The principal object of the survey was to consider the over-all organization structure, for improvements in the service, and not merely ways and means of cutting costs.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that survey has the right approach as regards the method of improving the service without reducing staff.
On the general over-all organization of the department we find these recommendations on page 16:
(f) Provide and arrange for the erection of letter boxes or other receptacles at such locations as he deems appropriate, in which mail or mailable matter may be deposited or stored.
I will have further comments to make upon that matter later. On pages 19-20:
That decentralization has gradually taken place through pressure of events.
The senior officials of the department raised the problem of the difficulty of carrying out adequate operational planning under adverse circumstances, as they were fully occupied in their daily routines, with no opportunities to appraise the over-all situation and plan for the future.
Then on page 21 you will find this:
This is common to all organizations operating on a stringent budget. The staff who should be dealing with long-term plans are called on to assist in meeting the peaks of normal operations, and gradually become so involved in routine matters that they are unable to carry out their planning function.
Steps have already been taken to deal with this problem by some appointments, headed by a special assistant to the deputy postmaster general.

However, it is apparent that the number of qualified staff presently available for this type of work is completely inadequate to deal with the problems encountered throughout the department.
Here again is shown the need for more staff, and an effort made to meet the situation by the appointment of a key official.
At page 27, under "Grades of Staff":
In an operation of the magnitude of the Post Office Department, it is essential to have a sufficient number of top level positions of adequate remuneration to provide the incentive to high calibre men to join the service and make it their career.
Then on page 33, section II:
The work of the operations branch has over the years increased to the point where the staff at all levels are overloaded with a multitude of routine problems and correspondence. No one has had time to develop policies which can be applied on an over-all basis.
Then on page 34 under the heading of "Adequacy of Staff":
It is essential that detailed consideration be given to new construction in order that the most efficient operating methods be incorporated in the designs. Quite properly, the postal superintendent in charge of the buildings division has concentrated on this phase of his activities. All the staff in the division have been so engaged and they have not had time to seek out and introduce operating economies throughout the existing post offices. Our survey has disclosed that there is room for substantial savings through better lay-out, equipment and control.
Then on page 35, under "Equipment and Material Handling":
Certain improvements in equipment or methods which have been introduced in some post offices have not been made available to other offices as there is no machinery to pass on the experience gained or to ensure that the most efficient methods are used throughout the organization.
Our examination has indicated that there is opportunity for substantial savings if the best use were made of staff and equipment.
Controls.
The branch is operating under severe handicap as there are no standards established to measure the relative efficiency of a given method of operation. The lack of such standards is particularly felt when requests are received for additions to staff or accommodation. The lack of such a standard also makes it difficult to appraise the benefits which might be obtained from improvements in methods and equipment.
On page 37, under "Mechanical Engineering Division":
This division should make detailed examination of the equipment and lay-out presently in use. This study will disclose great differences in equipment. Equipment installed many years ago is still being used, although more efficient equipment is available, and no attempt has been made to standardize it.
On page 39, under "Postal Service Division -Letter Carrier Service", we find this. I may say that this is one matter in which we are all vitally interested.
There is a need for a re-appraisal of the services being provided at various centres across the country.

The department should be continually examining the nature and extent of services provided, and he prepared to make alterations to keep pace with changing conditions.
At pages 39 and 40, under "Revenue, Post Office Division":
It is essential that this division should delegate operating responsibility and authority to the field organization. At the present time, decisions are based on information collected in the field. This results in voluminous correspondence, and delayed action. In many cases, the men who collected the information in the first instance are in the best position to make the decisions.
I would add this. There is in the department nothing more disconcerting and more demoralizing than to have suggestions offered by the staff with regard to various improvements either ignored or not acted upon. Under "Methods and Procedures", on the same page we find this:
The staff available for this work has proved inadequate, and the existing manuals were in many cases issued years ago and are now to a large extent obsolete.
The production of up-to-date operating manuals should more than repay the expenditure involved in staff salaries required to prepare them. At the present time, there are numerous errors occurring throughout the service, and the correction of each one requires the expenditure of time and labour. Clear instructions should do much to reduce the number of errors.
It should be quite apparent to anyone who is on the operations staff that that would be good business and would be a good method of improvement. Here again is failure to take full advantage of information gained and to introduce needed improvements. On page 42, under "Workshops":
It was noted during our survey that a number of these workshops have extended their activities to the manufacture of equipment, such as cupboards, waste paper containers, binneys and skids, and to the repair of typewriters and other office equipment. These workshops were not established for this purpose, and it is questionable if this type of work is economical.
At pages 43-44, under "Time Study- Equipment Design":
One of the time consuming tasks in the post office is arranging letters on their arrival so that the addresses can be read and the stamps cancelled, -the "facing-up" and "primary sortation" operation. The use of conveyor belts and changes in equipment would allow two operations to be combined. While this plan will require further development, there is an indicated annual saving in the forward letter section of the Toronto post office alone of approximately $200,000 per annum.
Work Place Layout
In our opinion there is a tremendous scope for this work, and we feel that the benefits which would be derived would far outweigh the cost.

Here is a case where they venture to place the saving at 20 per cent. At page 49, under section III, "Transportation Branch-Planning":
Pressure is continually brought to bear on the branch by the public, or through their parliamentary representatives, to institute new services, or to extend existing services. The officials investigate these proposals and finally accept or reject the individual submissions.
These decisions are often difficult, for while the cost of providing a service can be calculated, the benefits are not easy to evaluate. This has left the branch in a position of continually taking a defensive stand in regard to new proposals.
Little effort has been made to appraise the whole transportation problem, and to develop a rational plan or policy to govern future operations and methods. This lack of planning appears to be the most serious shortcoming of the branch.
At page 57, under "Establishment and Extension of Services":
The department in many cases has not considered the establishment of completely new services, or the extension of existing services until public demand has drawn their attention to the need for such action. This has resulted in the services varying according to the demands of the public in various parts of the country.
There should be a constant review of the services to be in a position to anticipate complaints.
At page 57, under	"Transportation-
Within Cities":
A limited survey of conditions in Toronto disclosed that the planning of this pick-up and delivery service had not been given the consideration which it deserves. A careful planning of routes and scheduling of services should reduce the transport required by the contractor, and the time the transport would be in use, thus reducing the cost to the department. In larger cities, where continued changes in traffic regulations are being made, this is a full time job. Officers should be appointed to study this problem.
The last three quotations I just read from pages 49 to 57 give a fair and impartial summation of what has happened generally, but particularly in suburban areas, and the members representing such ridings know the end result thoroughly, because they are constantly approached by their constituents to improve these services of which they are so sadly in need and to which they are entitled. On page 58 rural mail couriers are dealt with as follows:
This question has many broad aspects, and a clearer policy seems indicated. It would include further developments on standards of service, and the possible introduction of fulltime couriers employed, and provided with motor transportation.
I will go further here and make the comment that in the report reference was made to the fact that there was supposed to be a study of the situation with regard to rural mail delivery by a committee of the house. But that was not pursued further and no action was taken with the exception that an

Post Office Act
increase was granted to them. That has been the only action so far. There still has not been any investigation of the conditions under which rural mail couriers find themselves. On pages 76 and 77, in section V dealing with the administration branch, there are the following observations and comments under the heading "Financial and Statistical Controls":
It has been recognized in the department for some time that there is a lack of information on which to base policy decisions and control activities. The only existing data which can be used to compare the operations of two post offices is the dollar revenue received by post offices. This is not an adequate measure of the volume of work performed by each. This lack of information is particularly felt when additional staff or space is requested. It is not possible to decide whether these requests are justified by comparison with other similar operations.
A cost division has been established to devise a practical method whereby the cost of handling various types of mail could be established or estimated. It has made some progress and each year reduces the cost of the various postal service estimates.
On pages 77 and 78 there is the following:
During recent months a few of the larger post offices have been asked to estimate their expenditures in advance and submit monthly reports comparing their actual expenditures with these estimates. It is recommended that the development of controls be pushed forward vigorously.
The immediate goal should be the production of regular monthly statements for the various operations in the major post offices showing:
(i)	Actual expenditures for the period on an over-all and unit basis for each operation.
(ii)	Similar figures for the same period in the prior year.
(iii)	The budget figures for the period.
The information contained in the monthly statements of individual post offices should finally be compared on a unit cost basis and differences investigated.
These are some of the salient points picked at random from the survey, a selection of opinions, observations and recommendations, and a fair summary of them would be that there is no system or method of breakdown to determine the cost of each operation within the postal service; that decentralization has taken place by the very force of circumstances and not by any conscious policy of the department; that the survey is interspersed with comments on the lack of competent personnel and the need for modern equipment, and because of this the senior officials cannot solve the many problems confronting them, let alone carry out adequate operational plans; that this lack of planning is evident, whether caused by neglect, pressure of work or complete indifference; that work has increased to the point where the staff at all levels is overloaded with a multitude of routine problems and correspondence, and no one has had time to develop policies and the situation has produced a catalogue of deficiencies.

I shall now revert to page 18 and the chart of the organization set up for the top level- the Postmaster General, the deputy postmaster general, a chief executive officer to be assistant to the deputy minister, and a special assistant. Their duties are also defined. The one I am interested in is the special assistant whose position is defined on page 18 in these words:
There Is also a special assistant who has been carrying out special assignments of a planning nature.
All through the survey it is indicated that there is a pressing need for such an official. How long has he been appointed and where has he been? In the face of the facts presented, is this lack of staff again, or is it a question of too late and too little? The survey reveals that some changes have been in operation for some time, that some have just been initiated and that the remainder are in the realm of probable outcome. While the survey implies that a reduction of staff will result in certain instances, these people can be absorbed by transfer and promotion to departments now undermanned, and an abundance of opportunities will be provided for ambitious personnel with talent to aspire to higher positions.
It is now abundantly clear that we have established our claim that the government has made a major error in introducing a bill to increase postal rates before effecting the reorganization of the department. We are entitled to have the plan of reorganization tried out before the imposition of the proposed increases in rates, and to insist upon these increases before the plan has had a fair trial is an affront to the people of this dominion. Let me state that all through the survey positive statements have been made by the consultants that savings can be made. Such assertions are repeatedly made, and the report even goes so far as to say that the savings would amount to approximately $1 million.
When the minister presented his statement today supplementing what he had previously said, he said he had been further advised by the consultants that the proposed changes to be put into operation would result in an increased cost to the department of over $700,000 and that this would be an added burden on the department. This advice is not contained in the survey. It clearly indicates and points out where savings can be made. As far as the increase in staff is concerned, I do not think it is going to be as great as mentioned. I think that men of talent required for the top level positions will be produced, and you will have to establish a training school to develop them.

It seems to me that no attention is being paid to the development of staff for future use. It has not been established when the service deteriorated into a deplorable state. The fault is attributed to no one and I am trying to find out whether there is not some person in the department to whom some vestige of responsibility can be attached.
The only place in the survey where I can find any indication is where reference is made to the appointment of a special assistant to the deputy minister. In fairness to him, the only thing that remains to be established is when he was appointed and what time he has had to accomplish the improvements mentioned as being necessary in the survey. I would say that this survey, on the face of it, is a wonderful one. It is not a woebegone chant or the lament of selected Jeremiahs trying to establish that there is something wrong with the operation. It is surprising that the postal department has been so good and has provided us any service at all in view of the handicaps under which it has had to operate.
If further staff were provided and the improvements implemented, the increased revenue that would result would more than make up for any loss caused through the adoption of the 40-hour week and increased wages for the mail carriers. On the face of this survey I say that the government has been ill-advised, and commits an outrage on the intelligence of men who are supposed to be of $10,000 a year calibre by putting this kind of proposition forward without first putting into effect the improvements which the report says can be accomplished. I think that this should be further questioned, and that the minister would be well advised to impress upon his colleagues that this is the time to show, for once, a little intelligence. I believe this bill should be withdrawn until such time as the minister has an opportunity of convincing them that there will be surpluses instead of the deficits that have been predicted.

speechtext:
We
have heard from a number of members in the house, and we have seen quite a number of brickbats thrown across the chamber at the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote). This has been true, not only in this session but in previous sessions, and I have probably thrown some myself. Before I throw any this afternoon, I want to publicly express my appreciation of the co-operation which I have received from the Postmaster General's department, and particularly the Toronto postmaster, with regard to cases I have brought to their attention.
Post Office Act
I have found the postmaster at Toronto and the postal officials here, particularly since the present Postmaster General took office, quite ready to investigate any case which I have referred to them. I have had occasion to refer complaints about delay in mail delivery; I have had occasion to refer complaints about the time of the delivery; complaints about the location of post office boxes; complaints about the inadequacy and unsuitability of sub-post offices in my riding; and in each and every instance I found the department ready to investigate the complaint. I think that wherever there was justification for the complaint, or where the service was suffering by reason of these particular circumstances, changes have been introduced and improvements made. I find that the tension which existed, certainly two years ago, as between the general public and the Post Office Department on the one hand, and as between the postal employees and the Post Office Department on the other, has lessened considerably.
I keep in fairly close touch, both with the postal employees and with the service rendered by the post office in my constituency. I have every reason to believe that there is much less dissatisfaction today with the service being rendered, certainly than there was one or two years ago. I have often wondered just how the post office functions as well as it does, considering the frequency with which postmasters general are changed. Since I have been here I would say that no postmaster general has1 ever held that office long enough to really acquaint himself with the business of the post office-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext: They get promoted.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE POSTAGE ON LETTERS AFTER APRIL 1, 1954
speechtext:
-or to take any effective action towards improving that service. I do not know who runs the post office. Certainly, it is not the postmasters general, because they never hold the position long enough to become acquainted with the post office. I do not know why cabinet ministers do not want to hang on to that position longer. It may be because there are so many headaches in it that just as soon as they find out how many headaches there are they want some other cabinet position or some promotion. Certainly, I would think that is the basis of much of the trouble in the Post Office Department. I would recommend to the cabinet that once they get a good Postmaster General they keep him in that job for a while and give him an opportunity to do something.
The bill before us is based on two theories. The first theory is that the post office should

Post Office Act
be placed on a paying basis. I think that is a basic question that the house and the government should consider. I believe it is one of the questions that a committee such as is recommended in the amendment could investigate at some length, and a question about which we could get more than the opinions of postal officials themselves. I suspect this idea that the post office should be maintained strictly on a paying basis is a tradition that has grown up over the years amongst postal officials, and one that has not received very careful examination. For the life of me, I do not see why the post office should be singled out as the one public service that should be placed on a paying basis.
I do not see why the post office, for instance, any more than the Department of National Health and Welfare should be on a paying basis. It is a service department. I have not heard anyone suggesting that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) should collect enough revenue to offset all the expenses of his department. The mines branch of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is rendering a service to the mining operators in all parts of this country. I have never heard any suggestion that that department should collect from these mining companies enough fees to offset the expenses of the department. The whole question is, why should the post office be the one department of government rendering a public service that should pay its way? I think it is a fundamental question that should be examined.
The second point, of course, is the statement by the Postmaster General that the users of this service should pay for it. Even if you accept the theory that the over-all service rendered by the Post Office Department should be paid for by those who use the service, in other words that the revenue coming into the post office should be sufficient to offset the total expenditures, there are groups of people being served whom it would not be in the interests of the country generally to require to pay for the service.
About two years ago, I believe, the government brought in an amendment to the Post Office Act to increase the rates on second class mail. There was a flood of propaganda from newspapers and magazines against the original government proposals, and the consensus in this house and, I believe, in the country was that by enabling Canadian citizens to receive newspapers and magazines at a lower cost than the actual cost of carrying them, and thereby keeping down the price of those newspapers and magazines to the public, the government was rendering a

public service. If I remember correctly the government, in the face of that propaganda, modified their original suggestions regarding the rate that was to be charged. I quote that as one example to prove that we certainly do not expect the users of the post office to pay the whole cost of the service. We do not expect the editors and publishers of newspapers and magazines, nor do we expect the individual subscribers to those papers and magazines, to pay the whole cost of the postal service.
I just cannot see why one group of people who use the services, the group who use the first-class mail service, should be called upon to carry the deficits which result from giving other users a service below cost, especially in the light of the fact that the users of first-class mail are the one group of users of the public service who not only pay for the service they get but every year contribute a considerable surplus to help carry other branches of the post office service.
I am going to support the amendment. I am sure that as far as his office is concerned the present Postmaster General has no greater ambition than to see that that service is maintained on as efficient a basis as possible. I would think that the Postmaster General would welcome the setting up of a committee before which he and some of his officials could appear, and at which a study of the whole administration of his department could be made. If the department is administered as efficiently as the minister would have us believe it is, surely he has nothing to fear from the investigation of such a committee. I would think it would be a feather in his cap to have a committee set up and to have his officials come before it and to find out that he has the most efficiently run department in the government service.
If on the other hand we can discover ways and means of improving this service, I am sure that the minister would welcome any suggestions along that line. We are told that there is nothing perfect. It is just possible that the administration of the post office may not be perfect in every respect. It is just possible there may be ways of improving it; and if by the type of investigation that is visualized by the mover of this amendment we can improve that service to the public, then by all means let us do it. I hope the minister will consider the possibility of having such an investigation.

should like to say a word in respect to the amendment. The charge has been made that we have political patronage in our postal department. I for one feel that the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart)

was certainly right on the beam when he said that. We find it apparent everywhere. We need only go to our own particular ridings and examine some of the incidents and we shall find probably no end of them.
Perhaps it is a coincidence that in my particular riding the post office at Newton-it is a rather small one-should have required a new postmaster this year. I would not charge that this was a particular case of political patronage. There are about six or eight boxholders in that Newton post office, and it does a very substantial business. The reason it is doing such a substantial business is that the area surrounding the post office has a rural route, and naturally these people have to get their mail through the rural route. They buy their stamps and their postal notes, and so forth, at their nearest post office, which all helps the post office business.
Apparently, under the existing act the only people who can apply for a postal position of that particular kind are those who happen to get their mail at that post office. War veterans wanted to apply for the position but because they happened to live around the area, perhaps not more than 50 yards or 100 yards from it, and were on the rural route, they became ineligible. I wrote a letter to the postal officials and explained the situation but apparently the rules prevented them from changing the system. We found that a young man who was not a war veteran-I do not say that we must necessarily put war veterans in every position-got the position, since there were only one or two other applicants eligible and they were found to be, shall I say, of an inferior nature.
Another instance that I have in mind has to do with the post office that serves my own community. Some three or four years ago we had occasion to require a larger postal outlet. The people in the community knew nothing about the post office until it practically became a reality. Mr. Speaker, I was pleased half an hour ago to have the first really possibly valid explanation why this new tax is necessary. That possible explanation was that there has been such a thing as absentee landlordism, which we all know is never a good business proposition. We in this section of the house would not hesitate to support the government if it could establish any need for a tax. However, after listening all the days that we have spent on this I find that nothing has come forward. I have watched the newspapers from one end of Canada to the other, and I have not noticed any newspaper openly coming out and saying that the government needs to impose this new tax.
I noticed the sympathy that was expressed for the little man. I think the statement was "pity the little man." This tax is a tax on the general public of Canada. It is a tax on the little man. I believe it was the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) who pointed out that even though big business may initially pay most of this tax, in the long run it is added on to the cost of goods and services, and is in effect a tax on the little man.
I find it rather amusing that this government should now come to parliament at this time, taking into consideration the state of its finances, and say that it needs additional revenue. I do not think the government has proved that it needs additional revenue at all. It says that the post office must pay its way. Well, assuming, although I am unwilling to do that, that it is a valid argument that the post office must pay its way, how can you ask us to supply the post office with additional

revenue if within the post office there are major divisions that are not paying their way? I am referring once more to the subsidization of advertising. I maintain that if advertising paid its fair share of operating our post office, the government would have a much larger surplus next year than they had last year. As I indicated on January 14, if advertising were made to pay its fair share the government would be doing the country a good service in many other ways besides helping out the revenues of the post office.
I am not going to say much more. I was pleased that the first solid argument has now been presented, and I would recommend that the difficulty can be easily avoided next year if our genial Postmaster General would remain in Ottawa during the coming fiscal year and help out in that way. I am wondering whether this idea in the post office originated during the term of the absentee landlordism. I notice that the Secretary of State is a pupil of a former prime minister of Canada who, despite a large majority, rode out of power on the philosophy of "not a five-cent piece". Perhaps that philosophy has been taken up by the pupils and this government, even though it now has a large majority, may not go out on a five-cent piece, but on a five-cent postage stamp at the time of the next election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are asked to approve an increase in postal rates on letters ranging from 25 per cent to 50 per cent, and the increase is to apply only to letters posted in Canada and delivered in Canada. I suppose the result will be that first-class letters which will require five cents in Canada will require only four cents when sent abroad, which seems to me to be an initial breach of the proposition of payment according to service. I appreciate the fact that there may be international arrangements involved. That is the first thing I should like to point out.
My purpose is to consider for a moment the effect of the increase in rates on certain users. Like others, I have had a good many communications from individuals, mostly on limited fixed incomes, to whom this increase in rates will be a cost which they will feel. It does not seem much, but to those who are confined to limited quarters and maintain their communications by letter writing, it is a consideration. I might add that in my riding are located Eaton's mail order house at Albert and Bay streets and Simpson's mail order house on Mutual street. Those companies will not be affected by the increase because they mostly use parcel post and I do not note that
Post Office Act
the parcel post rates are to be increased. The letters which they receive will be from their customers who will have paid the postage.
I would not think that other business will be greatly concerned with this increase because postage is an ordinary cost of doing business which is deductible from income before taxation. Although there is some increase in the cost, in the case of a corporation half of that would be borne by the federal treasury in loss of taxation. That would minimize the increase in these cases.
Nevertheless postage is a cost of doing business. I suggest to the minister and to the house that all costs of doing business in this country, which was described recently in very authoritative terms by Mr. James Muir of the Royal Bank of Canada as a high-cost economy, are worthy of consideration, whether they are large or small. This is particularly so when one considers our competitive position in export markets which is of vital importance to every Canadian.
If postage is an element of cost it seems to me the sound principle upon which to approach postage rates is the maintaining as far as possible of rates that are comparative with those of our nearest neighbour and competitor, the United States of America. We all know that their rates are lower and the divergence will be even greater. There has been the suggestion that Canadians living near the border will cross and use the United States mails in order to save money.
In any event that is a factor and it raises a principle which to my mind is more important than the principle advanced to support this bill, namely, the principle of maintaining competitive costs in this particular element of the cost of doing business. The house is well aware that the principle advanced by the government is that those who use the service should pay for the benefits which they receive. It has been pointed out many times that that principle is not one which is observed in many other governmental activities.
I have not heard the minister estimate what may be the loss in revenue due to the increase in the rates. Undoubtedly many people who would have written letters and used the postal services for the transaction of some of their business will not do so because of the increased cost. As everyone knows, there is a point where the law of diminishing returns begins to have an effect and offset any increase in revenue. There may be a reduction in the number of letters that would otherwise be posted, but I have not heard any mention of that.

Post Office Act
In any event, if we accept the proposition, there has been no basis on which these principles could apply to the operations of the Post Office Department. The sole basis on which any accountant would work would be that the cost of operating the Post Office Department should be the actual costs. It is true that we are given a balance sheet but no one can see what the actual costs are because they do not appear there. Nor can anyone see what the potential revenues are.
I would suggest that this is a matter of rating. Rating is not a difficult problem when applied to this kind of utility service. We have the board of transport commissioners which fixes the rates to be paid for the carriage of passengers in different cars on the same trains in which letters are carried. If it is possible to arrive at a fair rate for the carriage of passengers, surely evidence could be produced to show the fair cost of providing a service to carry letters on trains. The same with carriage by air.
The same principle applies to telephone and telegraph rates. This form of communication is in close parallel to communication by letter, and we all know that the rates are fixed on evidence as to the cost of doing business plus a fair charge for the service rendered. If the minister is serious in wishing to apply cost accounting principles to the department over which he has the honour to preside, it appears to me that the means of doing so are available. It may be that he should now reconsider whether the Post Office Department should be disentangled from other departments of government and established as a separate agency or utility whose rates would be fixed on cost principles by a board capable of handling that kind of proposition.
This is big business. The revenues of this department last year were $129 million, at least those revenues shown in the statement, and we know that the department did not receive payment for all the services it rendered. The expenses shown, which we know were not the full expenses, amount to $122 million, leaving a surplus of something over $6 million.
This is the kind of business which could be handled very much in the way the Bell Telephone Company handles the telephone business of this country, or in the way the telegraph companies handle their business. It is not too large in proportion to those businesses. If the minister is serious about this proposition, he could find many advantages in having the Post Office Department operated by a utility agency. He would then be sure that it was being operated at cost or at a profit, and the Department of Public Works would
[Mr. Michener.I
be in receipt of revenues for the buildings occupied by the Post Office Department. The department would be compensated for the services it rendered on a businesslike basis, which is to my mind the only justification which the government has attempted to put forward in support of this measure.
I suggest it would be an interesting speculation if the minister were to call for tenders for the operation of the postal services at the existing rates and find how many people would be ready to come forward and say that with efficient operation they could handle the mails of this country without increasing the rates. That of course is speculative, but it is no more speculative than the application of the principle upon which we are asked to approve this bill.
I have made it clear that I cannot vote to approve this increase in rates. I should like to conclude by giving one trifling example, but it is an example of what some government agencies are not doing to keep the cost of the postal service as low as possible. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
General
The initial step in the implementation of our report on the organization and administration of the department will be to enlist the support of the senior officials in the department. It will also be necessary to obtain the approval of the civil service commission and the treasury board.
Detailed establishments of some of the new divisions will have to be developed. It is difficult in the initial stages to accurately estimate the final requirements for clerical staff and it will be necessary to review these requirements after the new organization has been in operation for a trial period.
One of the first steps should be the appointment of a personnel director. He should be supplied with a small staff possibly borrowed from some of the other branches and immediately undertake a study of the following matters:
(i)	Personnel available for immediate appointment to the new positions.
(ii)	Personnel who, after training, would be suitable for appointment to the new positions and the training they will require.
(iii)	What positions will have to be filled from outside the department.
The various changes in organization suggested in the report are set out below by branches with comments as to the timing.
Operations Branch
(a)	Chief superintendent-engineering-A man should be obtained from outside the service to fill this vacancy. It can be filled as soon as a suitable candidate is available. There is no need to delay any other moves in the interval.
(b)	Mechanical engineering division-This position should be filled either from outside the service or possibly by one of the engineers from the major post offices. The balance of the staff should be recruited either outside or from within the department but at least one engineer should come from one of the major post offices. This division can be organized as soon as personnel are available.
(c)	Methods and time study division-A start should be made immediately on the organization of this division. Either the man to head the division or one or two of his
assistants should be drawn from outside the department. A study should be undertaken of one of the major post offices and standards developed. The staff can be enlarged over a period of time as experience is gained and after suitable training could be drawn from within the department or, if suitable personnel are not available, from outside.
(d)	Chief superintendent-operations-This position should be filled by the most experienced man available within the service. He probably should be drawn from the field organization and might well be a successful district post office inspector.
(e)	Postal services division-This division will be made up of personnel presently in the branch. It can be set up as soon as a suitable postal superintendent is available.
(f)	Revenue post office division-The removal of functions from this division will be dependent on the completion of the organization of the postal services division and the district offices.
(g)	Methods and procedures division-The organization of this division is dependent on obtaining suitable personnel to carry out the work. This should be given a high priority and they should, if possible, be drawn from the field.
(h)	Inquiries division-As soon as a suitable postal superintendent can be selected, this division can be formed. A post office inspector would be most suitable for this position. The personnel in the inquiries section of the inspection division would form the staff.
(i)	The staff post office division would be transferred out of this branch to the personnel branch as soon as the personnel director is ready to receive it. It would form the nucleus of the employee services division in that branch.
Transportation branch
(a)	Chief superintendent - transportation planning and research-This position should be filled as soon as possible. It is important that the right man be selected as the success of the proposal will depend to a large extent on the imagination and energy of the individual chosen. The mail transportation officers presently on the staff would form the

nucleus of the chief superintendent's staff. A man with experience in commercial transport operations should be obtained from outside the service and added to the staff.
(b)	Chief superintendent - transportation services-This position should be filled by a man with proven administrative ability.
(c)	Motor vehicle services division-As soon as a postal superintendent has been selected from within the department, this division can be established, drawing its staff from the other divisions in the branch.
(d)	Account verification division-This division can be established as soon as the postal superintendent is selected. He could be drawn from either the transportation or finance branches.
(e)	The tender section can be reorganized and the new routines established as soon as the chief superintendent, transportation services, has been appointed.
Financial branch
(a)	There are three senior positions to be filled in this branch and the organization changes can take place as soon as suitable men are available. In addition there is the position of comptroller in the administration branch. It will probably be necessary to go outside the department to fill two or three of these four positions.
(b)	With the exception of the recommendations in connection with-
(i)	Preparation and recording of salary warrants,
(ii)	Punch card accounting machines,
(iii)	Post office savings banks,
all the recommendations in the section of the report on the financial branch can be proceeded with without delay under the direction of the director. The recommendations in connection with the preparation and recording of salary warrants and punch card accounting machines will have to be postponed until the district offices are ready to assume the additional responsibility. The recommendations in connection with the post office savings bank are subject to policy approval from the government.
Administration branch
(a)	Inspection division-The changes in organization of the inspection division and the change in the method of operation is dependent on the revision of the field organization. It is contemplated that the changes in the field organization will take place progressively one district at a time. As the change is completed in each district the
Post Office Department inspection branch would change its function in that district. The reorganization of the division at headquarters would be dependent on these developments.
The inquiries section can be transferred to the operations branch as soon as a postal superintendent is selected to head the new division.
The recommendations in connection with the misdirected mail office can be implemented forthwith.
(b)	Comptroller-As stated above, it may be necessary to go outside the department to fill this position. In the proposed plan for decentralized operations, the financial controls will be very important. It is essential that the man chosen to fill this position be imaginative and aggressive and have good accounting qualifications.
As soon as the comptroller is appointed, the budgets, estimates and costs division can be formed absorbing the personnel from the cost ascertainment division and the personnel of the staff relations division presently dealing with estimates.
A postal superintendent should be appointed to take charge of the statistical and office services division and the balance of the staff would be drawn from the other divisions as work is taken over. This can be commenced as soon as the postal superintendent is appointed. Consideration might be given to appointing the postal superintendent in charge of the cost ascertainment division to this post and filling the vacancy in the budgets, estimates and costs division with a younger man chosen from the department or outside.
(c)	Domestic mails division-The suggested illegal mail section can be formed from the staff of the dead letter office in Ottawa at any time.
(d)	International mails division-The reorganization of this division should take place at the same time as the accounting duties are transferred to the statistical and office services division. This will be dependent on the organization of that division.
(e)	Purchasing and stationery division- Approval of the treasury board of the suggested new limits of authority for expenditures will be required. The other recommendations can be proceeded with forthwith and do not affect the organization of the rest of the department.
Personnel branch
As already indicated the appointment of a director should be given priority.

speechtext:
Post Office Department
The first step in organizing this branch should be the transfer of the existing divisions dealing with personnel to the personnel director.
As already mentioned the staff post office division can be transferred at any time and would form the nucleus of the employee services division.
The training and welfare division can also be transferred at any time and would form the new training division.
The staff relations division can be transferred at any time and would form a section of the employee services division. As previously stated the personnel dealing with estimates would be transferred to the budgets, estimates and costs division.
The staff to form the personnel development division should, if possible, be drawn from within the department. There are undoubtedly a number of men in the training and welfare division, and the staff post office division who would be suitable and could be replaced in their present positions.
The organization of the division along the lines suggested can be carried out progressively over a period of time. It will not be completed until such time as the district offices are sufficiently organized to assume their additional responsibilities.
Field organization
The suggested changes in the field organization cannot be carried out all at once and it will take a number of years to complete.
It is suggested that the change-over be carried out on a progressive basis as follows:
(a) Select two districts as pilot operations.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
(b)	Select the district directors, the principal members of the district office staffs and the area superintendents.
(c)	Draw up detailed plans for the organization.
(d)	Plan a training course for the personnel involved which would stress the significance of the decentralization and the part each person is to play in it.
(e)	Send half of the staff for each of the new districts on the training course. As soon as they have completed the course the other half would be sent.
(f)	Establish the organization in the two districts.
(g)	Routines and procedures should be carefully developed in these two districts as they will become patterns for the whole department.
(h)	In the first instance, the new districts would carry on the same duties as are presently performing in the field but under the new organization, as the transition progresses further, duties and responsibilities will be delegated from headquarters.
(i)	The same steps would be followed progressively in each of the districts.
(j)	It is recommended that the deputy postmaster general appoint one senior man whose full time would be spent in coordinating this development.
(k)	The recommendations in connection with the four major post offices can be proceeded with immediately personnel are available.
